meta.description:
The medications in your selected treatment can have certain side effects, which you should be aware of before getting started.

## Finasteride

<Collapse title="Psychological side effects">
This type of medication may cause or worsen depression and anxiety.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Sexual side effects">
These may include decreased semen volume, decreased libido, and erectile dysfunction.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="How likely are side effects?">
While there is controversy, the possibility of persistent side effects exists, even after the medication is stopped.

Overall, sexual side effects occur in about 4% of patients taking medication versus about 2% taking a placebo (a "sugar pill"). For over 50% of patients, the side effects go away even if the medication is continued, and nearly always go away if stopped.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="What if I experience side effects?">
If side effects occur, no matter how mild or uncommon, it is vital to report them as soon as possible and consider stopping the medication.
</Collapse>

## Minoxidil

<Collapse title="Common side effects">Common side effects can include low blood pressure (hypotension) and swelling in the legs (edema), among others. Some people experience headaches, although those typically improve over time. Others may experience additional hair growth on the face or body (hypertrichosis). This is the most common side effect of taking oral minoxidil, though the complaint is more common among women than men and is also more common when taking over 5 mg per day.

Side effects of oral minoxidil may be more pronounced when the drug is prescribed at higher doses. For full safety information (including the boxed warning) read through the Important Safety Information here.</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Serious side effects">These serious side effects can occur with oral minoxidil. You or a caregiver should carefully monitor for these side effects, especially in the beginning of treatment and with dose changes.

- Salt and water retention: Monitor for fluid retention and increase in body weight. If you quickly gain five or more pounds, or if there is any swelling or puffiness in the face, hands, ankles, or stomach area, this could be a sign that you are retaining body fluids. Contact your Ro-affiliated provider or your in-person provider.
- Increased heart rate (tachycardia): You should measure your heart rate by counting your pulse rate while you are resting. If you have an increase of 20 beats or more a minute over your normal pulse, contact your Ro-affiliated provider or your in-person provider immediately.
- Pericarditis, Pericardial Effusion and Tamponade: Oral minoxidil can cause an accumulation of fluids in the sac surrounding the heart. Monitor for sharp pain in the chest, arm, or shoulder; signs of severe indigestion; or shortness of breath, dizziness, lightheadedness, and fainting. These could be signs of serious heart problems and you should seek immediate emergency care.
- Hazard of Rapid Control of Blood Pressure: A sudden or too large of a drop in blood pressure can lead to fainting, heart attack, and loss of blood flow to certain organs.</Collapse>

<Collapse title="How likely are serious side effects?">Oral minoxidil has not been extensively studied as a treatment for hair loss, and therefore we cannot say with confidence the exact percentage likelihood that someone may experience side effects. For more information on the side effects of oral minoxidil, please see the full Important Safety Information.</Collapse>

<Collapse title="What if I experience side effects?">If you notice side effects, let your healthcare provider know as soon as possible. They’ll be able to advise you about how you can use minoxidil safely. If you experience chest pain, chest tightness, or shortness of breath, stop taking minoxidil and let your provider know immediately. You or a caregiver should carefully monitor for side effects, especially in the beginning of treatment and with dose changes. For more information on the side effects of oral minoxidil, please see the full Important Safety Information.</Collapse>

Prior to reviewing your treatment request, your doctor or nurse practitioner will use your photos to verify your identity.

### How should I take the photo?

#### For ID:

If you add a driver’s license, take a photo of the front of the ID on a flat surface. If you add a photo of your passport, take a photo of the page with your picture on it.

Make sure your ID is well lit and clear – your doctor or nurse practitioner must be able to read your name and date of birth.

#### For photo of your face:

Please ensure your face is well-lit and not blurry, you are the only person in the photo, and nothing is covering your face, including sunglasses or a hat.

The medications in your selected treatment can have certain side effects, which you should be aware of before getting started.

## Finasteride

<Collapse title="Psychological side effects">
This type of medication may cause or worsen depression and anxiety.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Sexual side effects">
These may include decreased semen volume, decreased libido, and erectile dysfunction.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="How likely are side effects?">
While there is controversy, the possibility of persistent side effects exists, even after the medication is stopped.

Overall, sexual side effects occur in about 4% of patients taking medication versus about 2% taking a placebo (a "sugar pill"). For over 50% of patients, the side effects go away even if the medication is continued, and nearly always go away if stopped.
</Collapse>

<Collapse title="What if I experience side effects?">
If side effects occur, no matter how mild or uncommon, it is vital to report them as soon as possible and consider stopping the medication.
</Collapse>

## Minoxidil

<Collapse title="Common side effects">Common side effects can include low blood pressure (hypotension) and swelling in the legs (edema), among others. Some people experience headaches, although those typically improve over time. Others may experience additional hair growth on the face or body (hypertrichosis). This is the most common side effect of taking oral minoxidil, though the complaint is more common among women than men and is also more common when taking over 5 mg per day.

Side effects of oral minoxidil may be more pronounced when the drug is prescribed at higher doses. For full safety information (including the boxed warning) read through the Important Safety Information here.</Collapse>

<Collapse title="Serious side effects">These serious side effects can occur with oral minoxidil. You or a caregiver should carefully monitor for these side effects, especially in the beginning of treatment and with dose changes.

- Salt and water retention: Monitor for fluid retention and increase in body weight. If you quickly gain five or more pounds, or if there is any swelling or puffiness in the face, hands, ankles, or stomach area, this could be a sign that you are retaining body fluids. Contact your Ro-affiliated provider or your in-person provider.
- Increased heart rate (tachycardia): You should measure your heart rate by counting your pulse rate while you are resting. If you have an increase of 20 beats or more a minute over your normal pulse, contact your Ro-affiliated provider or your in-person provider immediately.
- Pericarditis, Pericardial Effusion and Tamponade: Oral minoxidil can cause an accumulation of fluids in the sac surrounding the heart. Monitor for sharp pain in the chest, arm, or shoulder; signs of severe indigestion; or shortness of breath, dizziness, lightheadedness, and fainting. These could be signs of serious heart problems and you should seek immediate emergency care.
- Hazard of Rapid Control of Blood Pressure: A sudden or too large of a drop in blood pressure can lead to fainting, heart attack, and loss of blood flow to certain organs.</Collapse>

<Collapse title="How likely are serious side effects?">Oral minoxidil has not been extensively studied as a treatment for hair loss, and therefore we cannot say with confidence the exact percentage likelihood that someone may experience side effects. For more information on the side effects of oral minoxidil, please see the full Important Safety Information.</Collapse>

<Collapse title="What if I experience side effects?">If you notice side effects, let your healthcare provider know as soon as possible. They’ll be able to advise you about how you can use minoxidil safely. If you experience chest pain, chest tightness, or shortness of breath, stop taking minoxidil and let your provider know immediately. You or a caregiver should carefully monitor for side effects, especially in the beginning of treatment and with dose changes. For more information on the side effects of oral minoxidil, please see the full Important Safety Information.</Collapse>

learnMore.description:
Disclaimer: This is not medical advice. You and your physician will determine if (and potentially how) you should take oral minoxidil.

The active ingredient in oral minoxidil is the same as the one in topical minoxidil (generic Rogaine). While topical minoxidil is FDA-approved to treat hair loss and is available without a prescription, oral minoxidil is considered “off label” and requires a prescription.

Oral minoxidil is FDA-approved (at higher doses) to treat high blood pressure. Doctors began prescribing low-dose oral minoxidil tablets as a convenient, once-a-day, non-hormonal hair loss treatment because in clinical trials studying higher doses of oral minoxidil for high blood pressure, a large percentage of patients experienced “elongation, thickening, and enhanced pigmentation of body hair,” including on the scalp.

Healthcare providers have the discretion to prescribe medications off-label if they believe it is an appropriate course of treatment for a particular patient.

While the exact mechanism is not completely understood, it’s thought to increase the length of the growth phase of hair follicles (a process called “anagen”) and increase the size of hair follicles, which is thought to promote hair regrowth.

Minoxidil is also thought to relax smooth muscle in blood vessel walls, causing them to widen and increase blood flow. This may be one of the ways that minoxidil works to stop or slow hair loss and, in some cases, maybe even regrow hair. 

Many patients find it easier to take one pill a day vs. applying a topical treatment twice a day. A simpler routine can help to improve treatment adherence and consistency (in other words, it’s easier to make and keep a daily treatment habit), which supports better results.

While the patient's preference is always taken into consideration, treatment recommendations will be primarily informed by your medical history as well as the side effect profiles of the individual treatments.

learnMore.description:
Disclaimer: This is not medical advice. You and your physician will determine if (and potentially how) you should take oral minoxidil.

The active ingredient in oral minoxidil is the same as the one in topical minoxidil (generic Rogaine). While topical minoxidil is FDA-approved to treat hair loss and is available without a prescription, oral minoxidil is considered “off label” and requires a prescription.

Oral minoxidil is FDA-approved (at higher doses) to treat high blood pressure. Doctors began prescribing low-dose oral minoxidil tablets as a convenient, once-a-day, non-hormonal hair loss treatment because in clinical trials studying higher doses of oral minoxidil for high blood pressure, a large percentage of patients experienced “elongation, thickening, and enhanced pigmentation of body hair,” including on the scalp.

Healthcare providers have the discretion to prescribe medications off-label if they believe it is an appropriate course of treatment for a particular patient.

The jury is still out on exactly how minoxidil works with regards to hair loss. While the exact mechanism is not completely understood, it’s thought to increase the length of the growth phase of hair follicles (a process called “anagen”) and increase the size of hair follicles, which is thought to promote hair regrowth.

Minoxidil is also thought to relax smooth muscle in blood vessel walls, causing them to widen and increase blood flow. This may be one of the ways that minoxidil works to stop or slow hair loss and, in some cases, maybe even regrow hair. 

Many patients find it easier to take one pill a day vs. applying a topical treatment twice a day. A simpler routine can help to improve treatment adherence and consistency (in other words, it’s easier to make and keep a daily treatment habit), which supports better results.

While the patient's preference is always taken into consideration, treatment recommendations will be primarily informed by your medical history as well as the side effect profiles of the individual treatments.

meta.description:
Oral Minoxidil can have certain side effects, which you should be aware of before starting treatment. Common side effects can include low blood pressure (hypotension) and swelling in the legs (edema), among others. Some people experience headaches, although those typically improve over time. Others may experience additional hair growth on the face or body (hypertrichosis). This is the most common side effect of taking oral minoxidil, though the complaint is more common among women than men and is also more common when taking over 5 mg per day.

Side effects of oral minoxidil may be more pronounced when the drug is prescribed at higher doses. For full safety information (including the boxed warning) read through the Important Safety Information here. These serious side effects can occur with oral minoxidil. You or a caregiver should carefully monitor for these side effects, especially in the beginning of treatment and with dose changes.
  • Salt and water retention: Monitor for fluid retention and increase in body weight. If you quickly gain five or more pounds, or if there is any swelling or puffiness in the face, hands, ankles, or stomach area, this could be a sign that you are retaining body fluids. Contact your Ro-affiliated provider or your in-person provider.
  • Increased heart rate (tachycardia): You should measure your heart rate by counting your pulse rate while you are resting. If you have an increase of 20 beats or more a minute over your normal pulse, contact your Ro-affiliated provider or your in-person provider immediately.
  • Pericarditis, Pericardial Effusion and Tamponade: Oral minoxidil can cause an accumulation of fluids in the sac surrounding the heart. Monitor for sharp pain in the chest, arm, or shoulder; signs of severe indigestion; or shortness of breath, dizziness, lightheadedness, and fainting. These could be signs of serious heart problems and you should seek immediate emergency care.
  • Hazard of Rapid Control of Blood Pressure: A sudden or too large of a drop in blood pressure can lead to fainting, heart attack, and loss of blood flow to certain organs.
Oral minoxidil has not been extensively studied as a treatment for hair loss, and therefore we cannot say with confidence the exact percentage likelihood that someone may experience side effects. For more information on the side effects of oral minoxidil, please see the full Important Safety Information. If you notice side effects, let your healthcare provider know as soon as possible. They’ll be able to advise you about how you can use minoxidil safely. If you experience chest pain, chest tightness, or shortness of breath, stop taking minoxidil and let your provider know immediately.
